Power to the People
POW-er too thuh PEE-pul
slogan (Boomer slang)
A radical slogan of the late 1960s associated above all with the Black Panther Party (founded Oakland, 1966), whose rallies chanted "All power to the people" by 1968–69; it was adopted across the student and anti-war left, and John Lennon released the single "Power to the People" in March 1971. The raised fist usually went with it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Power to the people was the cry of the late-1960s radical left: take power away from the government, the corporations, and the police, and hand it to ordinary people — usually through street protest, sometimes through revolution. The Christian observation: the slogan asks the right question, "Who has power?" and gives the wrong answer. Scripture’s answer is the first and last word on the matter: "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Our Lord told Pilate, the most powerful man in Judaea, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (Joh 19:11). Power is never the people’s by nature, nor the king’s; it is God’s, lent to men as stewards and answerable to Him. Scripture also shows what happens when power is simply handed to the people with no fear of God above them: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25), and the book of Judges ends in civil war and atrocity. Yet there is a power God does give to ordinary people, and freely: "as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God" (Joh 1:12), and "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you" (Act 1:8). That is the only power to the people that ever turned the world upside down without a single gun.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s radical slogan (Black Panthers; Lennon, 1971) demanding that power pass to ordinary people — answered by Scripture: power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11), who gives sinners power to become His sons (Joh 1:12).

POWER TO THE PEOPLE, slogan (Boomer era, late 1960s; Black Panther Party; John Lennon single, 1971) A demand that political and economic power be transferred from elites and institutions to ordinary citizens; often accompanied by a raised fist.

Webster (1828) — POWER, noun [The Latin has posse, possum, potes, potentia. The primary sense of the verb is to strain, to exert force.] 1. In a philosophical sense, the faculty of doing or performing any thing; the faculty of moving or of producing a change in something; ability or strength. A man raises his hand by his own power or by power moves another body. The exertion of power proceeds from the will, and in strictness, no being destitute of will or intelligence, can exert power power in man is active or speculative. Active power is that which moves the body; speculative power is that by which we see, judge, remember, or in general, by which we think. Power may exist without exertion. We have power to speak when we are silent. Power has been distinguished also into active and passive, the power of doing or moving, and the power of receiving impressions or of suffering.

Decode for families: the slogan is a theology of power with God left out. Ask your children, "Whose is the power?" and teach them Psalm 62:11.

Key Scripture

Psa 62:11 — "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God."

Joh 19:11 — "Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin."

Jdg 21:25 — "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Joh 1:12 — "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:"

Act 1:8 — "But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."

Modern Corruption

The slogan relocates sovereignty from God to the crowd; Scripture places all power in God, warns of every man doing right in his own eyes, and gives the people a better power — to become sons of God.

expand to see more

Every revolutionary slogan is a creed about where power comes from. The divine right of kings said it came from God to the king, and stopped there. Power to the people said it rises from the crowd, and stops there. Both are idolatries of a sort. The Reformed tradition, from Calvin through Rutherford’s Lex, Rex, held that power is God’s alone, delegated to magistrates under His law and answerable to Him, and that lesser magistrates may resist tyranny lawfully. That is very different from the street’s version, in which the crowd simply becomes the new king — and crowds have shouted both "Hosanna" and "Crucify him" in the same week.

Judges shows the end of the road: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25), and the people’s power produced the Levite’s concubine and the near-destruction of Benjamin. The gospel offers a different transfer of power. It does not take power from God and give it to man; it takes rebels and gives them power to become sons of God (Joh 1:12), and then sends them out with the power of the Holy Ghost (Act 1:8). Twelve unarmed men with that power did more to the Roman establishment than every raised fist of 1968.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin posse → Old French poeir → English power; Latin populus → people; late-1960s Black Panther chant → 1971 Lennon single.
